client: I've been really struggling lately because my professor assigned us this huge group project, and at the end of it we have to present in front of the whole class. Just thinking about standing up there makes my chest tighten and my mind go blank. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the presentation is still going to happen whether I feel better about it or not.
therapist:
It makes complete sense that your body is already reacting with that chest tightness — your mind is trying to protect you from something that feels genuinely threatening, and that's worth taking seriously. You're also right that the presentation will happen regardless, and I actually think that's a really grounded observation — our goal isn't to make the fear disappear, but to help you feel more capable of moving through it. 

When you imagine yourself standing up there and your mind goes blank, what's the thought or fear that feels most frightening — what do you picture happening next?

client: I picture everyone just staring at me in silence while I stand there completely frozen, and then I can see people starting to exchange looks like they think I'm an idiot. The worst part is that my group is counting on me, so if I mess up it's not just embarrassing for me, it's like I'm letting them all down too. That guilt on top of the fear is almost worse than the fear itself.
therapist: That image — frozen, being judged, and then feeling like you've failed the people who depend on you — carries so much weight, and it makes sense that the guilt feels almost heavier than the fear itself. I'd gently invite you to notice that your mind has written a very detailed story about what *will* happen, but I'm curious — when you think back on times you've felt this kind of dread before, how often did things actually unfold the way you feared they would? What evidence do you have, for or against, the idea that you're someone who lets people down?

client: Honestly, when I think back, things usually don't go as catastrophically as I imagine they will, but that doesn't really make me feel better right now because this situation feels different somehow. Like, in past situations the stakes felt lower, but here my grade and my group's grade are actually on the line, so the fear feels more justified this time. And I guess I don't have a lot of evidence that I let people down, but I also can't point to a time I've done something like this successfully, so the doubt just stays there.
therapist: You've just noticed something really important — that your mind is acknowledging the pattern of catastrophizing while simultaneously finding reasons why *this* time is the exception, which is actually a very common way anxiety keeps its grip on us. The absence of a clear success memory doesn't mean failure is likely; it might just mean you haven't yet had a chance to build that evidence, and this presentation could actually become that reference point you've been missing. What would it mean for you — and for how you see yourself — if this presentation went even just "okay" rather than perfectly?

client: I guess if it went just okay, that would technically be a relief, but part of me feels like "okay" still isn't good enough because my group deserves better than okay from me. It's like there's this voice that says anything less than impressive means I failed them, even if no one else would see it that way. I hear what you're saying about it becoming a reference point, but I'm not sure I'd actually let myself count it as a win even if it went fine.
therapist: That inner voice holding you to a standard that even a successful outcome can't meet — that's worth paying close attention to, because it means the goalposts are set up in a way where you almost can't win, no matter what happens. This sounds less like a realistic measure of what your group needs from you, and more like a rule your mind has created that keeps you in a constant state of not-enough. I'm curious — if a close friend told you they'd gotten through a scary presentation and their group passed, would *you* tell them that "okay" meant they'd failed everyone?

client: No, obviously I wouldn't say that to a friend, I'd probably tell them they were brave for getting through it at all. But it's so much easier to be kind to someone else than to apply that same logic to myself, and I don't really understand why that is. Like, I can see the double standard you're pointing out, but knowing it's there doesn't automatically make the voice any quieter.
therapist: You've just done something genuinely insightful — you can see the double standard clearly, and you're right that insight alone doesn't silence that voice, because that critical inner voice has likely had a lot more practice than the kinder one. The good news is that self-compassion is actually a skill that can be strengthened with practice, not just a feeling you either have or don't. I'm wondering — what do you think it would feel like to experiment, just once after the presentation, with deliberately saying to yourself exactly what you'd say to that friend, even if it feels a little forced or undeserved at first?

client: Honestly, it sounds kind of awkward and forced, like I'd just be saying words I don't actually believe yet, and I'm not sure that's not just lying to myself. I think the hard part is that if the presentation goes badly, trying to tell myself "you were brave" would feel hollow and almost insulting, like I'm just trying to paper over a real failure. I'm not saying I won't try it, but I guess I'm skeptical that it would feel genuine enough to actually stick.
therapist: Your skepticism is actually really healthy — you're not looking for empty reassurance, you're looking for something that genuinely holds up, and that tells me a lot about how thoughtful you are. It might help to reframe it less as "saying things you don't believe yet" and more as practicing a perspective that's actually *more* accurate than your inner critic's version, since we've already seen that voice sets impossible standards. What if the goal isn't to feel it fully right away, but just to stay open to the possibility that the kinder interpretation might be at least as true as the harsh one?

client: I think "at least as true" is something I can maybe sit with, because it doesn't feel like I'm being asked to pretend everything is fine. It's still hard to imagine actually remembering to do that in the moment after the presentation when I'm probably going to be flooded with either relief or dread. But I guess staying open to it is a smaller ask than fully believing it, so maybe that's a more realistic starting point for me.
therapist: That shift you just made — from "I have to fully believe it" to "I can stay open to it" — is actually a meaningful and real change, not a small one, even if it feels modest. One thing that might help bridge the gap between now and that flooded post-presentation moment is deciding *in advance* on one simple, specific thing you'll say to yourself afterward, so it doesn't have to be invented on the spot when your emotions are running high. What's one phrase that feels honest and manageable — not over-the-top, but genuinely fair — that you could have ready for yourself when that moment comes?

client: Maybe something like "I showed up and I did it," because that part would at least be factually true no matter how it goes. It feels plain enough that I wouldn't feel like I'm lying to myself, but I'm a little worried that in the moment it'll just sound pathetically low-bar, like I'm celebrating the bare minimum. I guess I can try to hold onto it anyway, even if part of me rolls its eyes at it.
therapist: "I showed up and I did it" is actually a quietly powerful statement, because showing up to something that fills your chest with dread and makes your mind go blank takes real courage — that's not a low bar, that's the whole battle. And honestly, the part of you that might roll its eyes at it is just that same impossible-standards voice we've already identified, so you can notice it without having to obey it. What do you think it says about you that even now, before the presentation has happened, you've been willing to sit with all of this discomfort and keep looking for a way through rather than just shutting down?

client: I guess it says something okay about me, though my instinct is still to brush that off and say I'm just doing what anyone would do. But maybe that's the same voice again, the one that won't let anything count. I didn't expect to actually get anything useful out of talking about this, so I'll admit this conversation has been a little more helpful than I thought it would be.
therapist: That instinct to immediately deflect — "anyone would do this" — is exactly that same voice, and the fact that you can catch it in real time now is genuinely significant progress. I'm really glad this felt more useful than you expected, and I want to reflect back that you came in skeptical, stayed honest throughout, and still did the hard work of examining your own thinking — that's not nothing, that's actually the whole process. As you carry "I showed up and I did it" into that presentation, I hope you'll also remember that you've already practiced something difficult today — what's one thing from our conversation you'd want to hold onto when the anxiety starts to rise before you walk up there?

client: I think the thing I'd want to hold onto is that the story my mind tells me about what's going to happen isn't the same as what will actually happen, because I've already seen that pattern today in how I was thinking. It's still going to be hard to remember that when my chest is tight and I'm about to walk up there, because anxiety has a way of making everything feel very certain and very real in that moment. But I think having that phrase ready, and knowing the voice that tears it down is the same unreliable one we talked about, gives me at least something to push back with.
therapist: What you just articulated — that anxiety creates a feeling of certainty that isn't the same as actual certainty — is one of the most important insights in understanding how anxiety works, and you arrived at it yourself, which means it's far more likely to stick than if I'd just handed it to you. You're walking away with a grounding phrase, a way to identify the critical voice, and a real understanding of your own patterns, and that's a genuinely solid foundation to stand on when that moment comes. I'll be rooting for you — and I hope afterward, you'll take a breath and let "I showed up and I did it" land for at least a moment before that voice gets a turn.
